analysis.one_liner: Charges oil, gas, and coal a rising fee per ton of emissions and sends most of the money back as household rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have charged a fee on carbon pollution — starting at $25 per ton in 2022 and rising $10 each year — on oil, gas, and coal, plus large industrial emitters. It would then return 75% of the money as quarterly rebate checks to adults, with payments phasing out for households earning over $75,000 ($150,000 for couples). The rest would fund a new government bank financing clean energy projects, $5 billion a year in transition aid to communities hurt by the decline of fossil fuel jobs, and payments to farmers for practices that store carbon in soil and trees. It also taxed imports from countries without comparable carbon pricing to protect U.S. factories, and paused the fee if unemployment was high.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households: each eligible adult would have received quarterly rebate payments, tax-free and not counted against other benefits, with the full payment for anyone earning under $75,000 ($150,000 for couples) and phaseouts above that. Because wealthy households use far more energy than low-income ones, most lower- and middle-income households would come out ahead. Also coal, oil, and gas communities — which would have gotten retraining, early-retirement subsidies, and cleanup grants — and farmers and forest landowners paid for carbon-storing practices.

how_it_helps.text: Starting in late 2022, every U.S. adult would get a quarterly 'carbon fee rebate payment' from the fund; 75% of fund money went to these rebates in the first 10 years, and payments phase out only above $75,000 in income for singles and $150,000 for joint filers [S3].
Rebates would be excluded from income taxes and not counted as income or resources for any federal or state benefits program, so receiving one could not cost someone food stamps or Medicaid [S3].

$5 billion in each of fiscal 2021 and 2022 would go to transition grants for communities hit by carbon-intensive industry job losses — including job training, a monthly early-retirement subsidy for affected workers, flood-proofing, and cleanup of coal ash, mines, and contaminated waterways [S3].

Farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners would be paid for practices like cover crops, conservation tillage, improved grazing, and reforestation that measurably reduce or store carbon, with payments sized to verified results [S3].

A new Climate Change Finance Corporation, capitalized with $7.5 billion a year for two years, would finance clean energy, electric transit and school buses, grid upgrades, carbon capture, and weatherization for low-income homes, prioritizing low-income, minority, Tribal, and deindustrialized communities [S3].

The carbon fee would rise automatically — $10 a year normally, faster if emissions targets were missed — aiming for a 45% emissions cut by 2030 and net zero by 2050, so the price signal could not be quietly repealed [S3].

Imported steel, cement, glass, chemicals, and fuels from countries without comparable carbon pricing would face an equalizing fee, and U.S. exporters would get refunds, so domestic manufacturers would not simply be undercut by dirtier foreign competitors [S3].
If unemployment in any census region was 5% or higher, the fee would be cut to zero for that quarter, keeping the tax from landing hardest during a downturn [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers — oil refineries, coal producers, and natural gas producers, plus importers of those fuels — would owe the fee and pass it along, so consumers would pay more for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity until the rebates arrived. Large industrial emitters (over 25,000 tons a year) would pay a separate fee. Wealthier households, who use more energy, would lose more in higher prices than they gained back in rebates. Importers of goods from countries without carbon pricing would face the border fee.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel companies, big industrial emitters, high earners

drawbacks.text: Energy prices would rise immediately while rebates arrive on a separate schedule, so some households would feel higher gasoline and utility bills before the offsetting check comes [S3].

Workers and businesses in oil, gas, and coal would face a shrinking market; the bill's response — transition grants — was capped at 10% of the fund and phased to zero after the first 14 fiscal years, while the fee kept rising [S3].
The unemployment safeguard could suspend the entire fee for a quarter in any economic downturn, repeatedly pausing the price signal and pushing the emission targets back [S3].
A carbon fee relies on accurate measurement of emissions by companies, verified by third parties the EPA certifies — a system that only works as well as its reporting rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the rebate is designed to exceed what they pay in higher energy prices, because low- and middle-income people use less energy than the wealthy — the bill is structured so the average household comes out ahead and the top income brackets come out behind. The real costs fall on fossil fuel producers and heavy industry, which is the point of the design. The most serious honest objections are the timing gap between higher prices and rebate checks, and the fact that transition aid for fossil-fuel-dependent towns phases out decades before the fee stops rising.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in August 2020, and with zero cosponsors it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on August 6, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list shows zero [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and there were no roll-call votes, floor votes, or hearings recorded in its action history [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal producers and large industrial emitters are better off because the fee never took effect; energy consumers never faced the price increases, and households never received the rebates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its carbon fee, household rebate, and community transition provisions; read twice and referred to Finance.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing or markup was held before the Congress ended.

against.name: United States Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill; no senator cosponsored it and no floor action occurred.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic senator introduced the bill late in a Republican-controlled Senate, no Republicans or additional Democrats signed on, and the Republican-led Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Covered entities — refinery operators, coal and natural gas producers, and fuel importers — would owe the fee on every ton of carbon in the fuel they sell, passed to consumers at the pump and utility bill. Killing the bill preserved the status quo for these companies.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: They would pay the fee on fuels and on industrial emissions above 25,000 tons a year, but the border adjustment would tax imports from countries without comparable carbon pricing and refund the fee on exports, shielding them from cheaper dirty competition. The bill's defeat spared them the fees but also ended the import protection.

industries.industry: Clean energy and clean technology industries
industries.note: The Climate Change Finance Corporation would have directed tens of billions into solar, wind, geothermal, batteries, electric vehicles and charging, hydrogen, and carbon capture — a large, sustained customer base the industry never got. Its interest runs alongside reducing the pollution affecting ordinary people.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and green banks
industries.note: Eligible lenders would have received federal guarantees of 75% of clean-energy project loans, pushing lending toward projects they might not otherwise finance. Modestly entrenching lenders as the channel for clean energy capital.
A decade of payments for verified practices like cover crops, rotational grazing, and reforestation would have opened a new revenue stream for agriculture and forestry tied to storing carbon.
Transition grants would have funded job training, early-retirement subsidies, coal ash cleanup, and mine reclamation in towns built around carbon-intensive industries.
